reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO
clinicalPearls: Caused by parvovirus B19 and most common in school-aged children, often occurring in community outbreaks
The typical rash begins with bright red cheeks giving a slapped-cheek appearance, followed by a lacy, reticular erythematous eruption on the limbs and trunk
The rash can wax and wane over weeks and may flare with warmth, sunlight, or exercise
By the time the rash appears the child is usually no longer infectious, since viral shedding peaks earlier during the mild prodrome
Adults, especially women, more often develop a symmetrical polyarthropathy affecting hands, wrists, and knees rather than a prominent rash
Because the virus targets erythroid precursors, it can precipitate transient aplastic crisis in patients with chronic haemolytic disorders and chronic anaemia in the immunocompromised
Infection in pregnancy carries a risk of fetal anaemia and hydrops fetalis, warranting fetal surveillance after maternal exposure
reference.pathophysiology: Parvovirus B19 is transmitted mainly by respiratory droplets and binds the P antigen (globoside) on erythroid progenitor cells, halting red cell production. In healthy hosts this transient arrest is clinically silent, and the exanthem and arthropathy that follow are largely immune-complex mediated, appearing as antibody develops. In people who depend on high red cell turnover the production arrest causes an acute aplastic crisis, while persistent infection in immunocompromised patients produces chronic anaemia. Transplacental infection can cause severe fetal anaemia and hydrops.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic lupus erythematosus (when arthropathy predominates in adults)
infectionMimics: Other viral arthropathies such as chikungunya or rubella-associated arthritis
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis usually adequate in a well child with the classic rash
Parvovirus B19 IgM and IgG serology to confirm recent infection, particularly in pregnancy or arthropathy
B19 DNA PCR in immunocompromised patients or when serology is unreliable
Full blood count and reticulocyte count where aplastic crisis is suspected
Fetal ultrasound surveillance for hydrops after maternal infection in pregnancy
redFlags: Sudden severe anaemia with a low reticulocyte count in a patient with an underlying haemolytic disorder (aplastic crisis)
Persistent anaemia or marrow suppression in an immunocompromised patient
Maternal infection in pregnancy with signs of fetal hydrops or anaemia
Profound pancytopenia suggesting a broader marrow process
reference.prognosis: In immunocompetent children and adults the illness is self-limiting with an excellent outcome, though adult arthropathy may linger for weeks to months; the serious outcomes are aplastic crisis in haemolytic disease, chronic anaemia in the immunocompromised, and fetal loss or hydrops in pregnancy.
pitfalls: Isolating the child once the rash appears, when infectivity has usually already passed
Missing an evolving aplastic crisis in a patient with sickle cell disease or other haemolytic anaemia
Overlooking recent parvovirus exposure as a cause of new symmetrical polyarthropathy in an adult
Failing to arrange fetal monitoring after documented maternal infection in pregnancy
management: Supportive care with antipyretics and analgesia in the immunocompetent, as the illness is self-limiting
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for the symmetrical polyarthropathy that predominates in adults
Reassurance that the child is generally no longer infectious once the rash appears, since viral shedding peaks during the earlier prodrome
Prompt red-cell transfusion and haematological monitoring for transient aplastic crisis in patients with chronic haemolytic disorders
Intravenous immunoglobulin for persistent parvovirus B19 infection causing chronic anaemia in the immunocompromised
In pregnancy, confirmatory serology with serial foetal ultrasound surveillance for anaemia and hydrops, and intrauterine transfusion with maternal-foetal medicine referral for severe foetal anaemia
Infection-control precautions to protect pregnant contacts and those with haemolytic disease
